gloss: The buying and selling of goods, stocks, or currency.
examples: *Trading* on the exchange stopped for an hour after the crash.
He made a small fortune in online *trading*.
*Trading* was light the day before the holiday.

gloss: Someone who is the first to do something and opens the way for others.
examples: She was a *trailblazer* for women in engineering.
The founders are considered *trailblazers* in solar power.
He called his old coach a real *trailblazer*.

gloss: Someone who is learning a job while working at it.
examples: She started as a *trainee* and now runs the department.
The bank hires about fifty *trainees* every summer.
A *trainee* shadowed me for the whole shift.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable: tray-NEE, not TRAY-nee.

gloss: The curved path an object follows through the air, or the general direction in which something develops.
examples: The rocket left its planned *trajectory* within seconds.
Her career has been on an upward *trajectory* since 2019.
The two countries are on very different economic *trajectories*.

gloss: A homeless person who travels from place to place.
examples: An old *tramp* was sleeping under the bridge.
The novel follows two *tramps* riding freight trains.
He looked like a *tramp* after three days of camping.

gloss: One portion of a larger sum of money, released or sold separately.
examples: The first *tranche* of aid arrives next month.
Investors bought the safer *tranches* of the loan.
The grant is paid out in three *tranches*.
contrast: Borrowed from French: the -che is said like sh, TRAHNSH.

gloss: A drug given to calm a person or animal down.
examples: The vet used a *tranquilizer* to move the injured bear.
He has been on mild *tranquilizers* since the accident.
The dart gun fires a *tranquilizer*.
contrast: American English spells it tranquilizer; British English writes tranquilliser.

gloss: A state of calm and quiet.
examples: We drove out to the lake for a weekend of *tranquility*.
Nothing disturbs the *tranquility* of that valley.
She found real *tranquility* in the monastery garden.
contrast: Americans usually write tranquility with one l; the British spell it tranquillity.

gloss: The process of changing from one state or system to another.
examples: The *transition* to the new software took three months.
Both *transitions* of power went smoothly.
She is in *transition* between jobs right now.

gloss: A device that sends out radio or television signals.
examples: Lightning knocked out the station's *transmitter*.
The researchers fitted the wolves with radio *transmitters*.
A tiny *transmitter* in the collar tracks the dog.

gloss: A device that receives a signal and automatically sends one back, used on aircraft and toll roads.
examples: The plane's *transponder* stopped sending data over the ocean.
Stick the toll *transponder* on your windshield.
Both *transponders* failed the preflight check.

gloss: The moving of people or goods from one place to another.
examples: The company handles the *transport* of frozen food.
Air *transport* is faster but far more expensive.
*Transport* of the equipment took two full days.
contrast: The noun is stressed TRANS-port, the verb trans-PORT. For the public system Americans normally say transportation.

gloss: Behavior that betrays someone who trusted you.
examples: He never forgave his brother's *treachery*.
The play is full of *treachery* and revenge.
She saw the leak to the press as pure *treachery*.

gloss: An exercise machine with a moving belt that you walk or run on.
examples: I do thirty minutes on the *treadmill* every morning.
All the *treadmills* at the gym were taken.
He hates running outside, so he bought a *treadmill*.
contrast: The first syllable is TRED, rhyming with bed, even though it is spelled like tread.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Gold, jewels, and other riches, or a single object of great value.
examples: Divers found buried *treasure* in the wreck.
The museum's greatest *treasures* are on the second floor.
That old map is a real *treasure*.

gloss: The person who looks after the money of a club, company, or organization.
examples: She was elected *treasurer* of the parent association.
Both *treasurers* signed the annual report.
Ask the *treasurer* how much is left in the fund.

gloss: A long, serious piece of writing on one subject.
examples: He wrote a *treatise* on constitutional law.
The library keeps medieval *treatises* on medicine.
Her essay reads more like a *treatise* than a blog post.
contrast: Spelled -tise but said with an s sound: TREE-tis.

gloss: A feeling of fear or worry about something that is about to happen.
examples: She opened the letter with some *trepidation*.
There was a lot of *trepidation* before the first day of school.
He approached the interview with obvious *trepidation*.

gloss: The offense of going onto someone's land or property without permission.
examples: He was arrested for *trespass* on railroad property.
The sign warns that *trespass* will be prosecuted.
The case turned on whether walking the trail counted as *trespass*.
contrast: The sign posted everywhere in the United States reads "No Trespassing", with the -ing form.

gloss: Strong loyalty to your own group, often combined with hostility toward outsiders.
examples: Commentators blame *tribalism* for the gridlock in Congress.
Sports *tribalism* is mostly harmless.
The article traces the rise of political *tribalism*.

gloss: The large muscle at the back of the upper arm.
examples: These push-ups work the *triceps*.
He tore his *triceps* lifting weights.
Her *triceps* are more developed than her biceps.
contrast: The singular already ends in -s, and the plural is also triceps.

gloss: A large plant-eating dinosaur with three horns on its head.
examples: The museum's *triceratops* skull is enormous.
My son can tell a *triceratops* from a stegosaurus.
Two *triceratops* skeletons came out of the same quarry.
contrast: The plural is normally the same as the singular: two triceratops.

gloss: A clever act done to entertain people or to deceive them.
examples: The dog knows three *tricks*.
That's an old *trick* salesmen use.
There's a *trick* to opening this window.

gloss: The use of dishonest methods to cheat or fool people.
examples: The contract was signed through outright *trickery*.
He won the game by skill, not *trickery*.
There was no magic in it, just *trickery*.

gloss: A spear with three points.
examples: The statue shows the sea god holding a *trident*.
Gladiators fought with nets and *tridents*.
The team's logo is a silver *trident*.

gloss: The number one million million, written 1,000,000,000,000.
examples: The national debt passed thirty *trillion* dollars.
*Trillions* of cells make up the human body.
The plan would cost about a *trillion* over ten years.

gloss: A set of three books or films that tell one connected story.
examples: I read the whole *trilogy* over the summer.
The studio is planning a *trilogy*.
Both *trilogies* were filmed back to back.

gloss: A three-legged stand that holds a camera or telescope steady.
examples: Set the camera on a *tripod* for night shots.
The photographers lined up their *tripods* along the fence.
I forgot the *tripod*, so every picture is blurry.

gloss: A great victory or success.
examples: The election was a personal *triumph* for the mayor.
The film was a *triumph* with critics.
She lists her small daily *triumphs* in a notebook.

gloss: A musician who plays the trombone.
examples: The band needs a second *trombonist*.
He is the best *trombonist* in the state.
Two *trombonists* stood up for the solo.

gloss: A state police officer, or a soldier in a cavalry or armored unit.
examples: A state *trooper* pulled us over near the border.
Two *troopers* blocked off the highway.
Her father was a *trooper* for twenty years.
contrast: Sounds exactly like trouper, a person who keeps going cheerfully: "she's a real trouper".

gloss: A familiar idea, image, or plot device that keeps turning up in stories.
examples: The lonely detective is a well-worn *trope*.
The show plays with classic horror *tropes*.
That's a tired *trope* about small towns.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Difficulty or worry, or a particular problem that causes it.
examples: He's in serious *trouble* at work.
The car gave us no *trouble* on the trip.
She listened patiently to all my *troubles*.

gloss: Someone who deliberately causes problems for other people.
examples: The teacher moved the two *troublemakers* apart.
He got a reputation as a *troublemaker* in high school.
Management labeled her a *troublemaker* after the walkout.

gloss: Staying away from school without permission.
examples: The district is trying to cut *truancy* in half.
*Truancy* rose sharply after the pandemic.
He was sent to court for chronic *truancy*.

gloss: An expensive underground fungus used in cooking, or a soft round chocolate candy.
examples: The pasta was shaved with black *truffle*.
She gave me a box of chocolate *truffles*.
Dogs are trained to sniff out *truffles*.

gloss: A musician who plays the trumpet.
examples: The *trumpeter* played the national anthem.
Miles Davis was the *trumpeter* everyone imitated.
Three *trumpeters* stood at the back of the stage.

gloss: A person appointed to manage money or property for someone else, or a member of a governing board.
examples: The board of *trustees* meets in April.
Her uncle is the *trustee* of the family fund.
Two *trustees* voted against the tuition increase.
contrast: Stressed on the last syllable, trus-TEE — unlike trusty, said TRUS-tee.

gloss: A small bunch of hair, grass, or feathers growing or held together.
examples: A *tuft* of white hair stuck up on the back of his head.
*Tufts* of grass grew between the paving stones.
The owl has dark *tufts* above its eyes.

gloss: A short, strong pull.
examples: She felt a *tug* on the fishing line.
Give the rope a couple of *tugs* when you're ready.
He felt a *tug* of guilt as he drove away.

gloss: A dry desert plant that breaks off at the root and rolls along the ground in the wind.
examples: A *tumbleweed* blew across the empty highway.
*Tumbleweeds* piled up against the fence overnight.
The town was so quiet you half expected a *tumbleweed*.

gloss: A very hard gray metal with an extremely high melting point.
examples: Old light bulbs used a *tungsten* filament.
The drill bits are tipped with *tungsten*.
His wedding ring is made of *tungsten*.

gloss: A loose garment reaching from the shoulders to the hips or knees, usually without a collar.
examples: She wore a linen *tunic* over leggings.
The actors wore Roman *tunics*.
His uniform *tunic* had brass buttons.

gloss: The chance to do something in an agreed order, or a change of direction.
examples: It's your *turn* to drive.
Make a left *turn* at the light.
The kids took *turns* on the swing.

gloss: A nasal quality in someone's accent, or the sharp sound of a plucked string.
examples: You can hear a slight Texas *twang* when she talks.
The guitar gave a metallic *twang*.
His voice lost its country *twang* after years in Boston.

gloss: A sudden short pain, or a brief uncomfortable feeling.
examples: I felt a *twinge* in my back when I stood up.
He had a *twinge* of guilt about leaving early.
The old injury still gives her *twinges* in cold weather.

gloss: A small flickering light, or a lively look in someone's eyes.
examples: He told the story with a *twinkle* in his eye.
We could just make out the *twinkle* of the town lights below.
There was a mischievous *twinkle* in her expression.

gloss: A small sudden movement of a muscle that you cannot control.
examples: He has a nervous *twitch* under his left eye.
The dog's ear gave a *twitch*.
Tiny *twitches* in his hands gave away how nervous he was.

gloss: A serious infectious disease caught from contaminated food or water.
examples: Travelers to the region are vaccinated against *typhoid*.
The outbreak of *typhoid* was traced to a single well.
She spent a month in the hospital with *typhoid*.
contrast: Typhoid and typhus are two different diseases, spread in completely different ways.

gloss: A serious infectious disease spread by lice and fleas, causing fever and a rash.
examples: *Typhus* swept through the camps that winter.
He died of *typhus* in 1943.
Crowded, dirty conditions helped *typhus* spread.
contrast: Do not confuse typhus with typhoid — despite the similar names they are separate diseases.

gloss: Someone whose job is typing documents.
examples: She worked as a *typist* in a law office.
The agency still employs two *typists*.
He's a fast *typist* but a terrible speller.

gloss: A ruler or boss who uses power cruelly and unfairly.
examples: The country was run by a *tyrant* for thirty years.
History books are full of *tyrants*.
Our old manager was a petty *tyrant*.

gloss: The quality of being unpleasant to look at, or of being nasty and hostile.
examples: He photographs the *ugliness* of the industrial coast.
There was real *ugliness* in the comments online.
The *ugliness* of the argument shocked everyone.

gloss: Light just beyond the violet end of the spectrum, invisible to the eye and able to burn skin.
examples: Sunscreen blocks most *ultraviolet* from reaching the skin.
The lamp gives off *ultraviolet* to kill bacteria.
Snow reflects a surprising amount of *ultraviolet*.

gloss: A piece of underwear worn on the lower body.
examples: Pack extra socks and *underpants*.
He walked to the kitchen in his *underpants*.
The store sells three pairs of *underpants* for ten dollars.
contrast: Plural only, like pants — one garment is "a pair of underpants".

gloss: A task or project, especially a large and difficult one.
examples: Rebuilding the bridge was a huge *undertaking*.
The move turned into a bigger *undertaking* than we expected.
Both *undertakings* ran well over budget.
contrast: Stressed un-dur-TAY-king in this sense; stressed UN-dur-tay-king it means the funeral business.

gloss: A quality or feeling that is present but not stated openly, or a very quiet voice.
examples: The speech had an angry *undertone*.
The comedy has surprisingly dark *undertones*.
They argued in *undertones* so the baby wouldn't wake up.

gloss: The world of organized crime, or the world of the dead in ancient myths.
examples: He spent years reporting on the city's *underworld*.
In the myth she travels to the *underworld* to find her husband.
The killing looked like *underworld* score-settling.

gloss: The cause of someone's failure or ruin.
examples: His temper was his *undoing*.
Overconfidence proved to be the team's *undoing*.
Greed was the *undoing* of the whole company.

gloss: The quality of treating people in a way that is not just or equal.
examples: Students complained about the *unfairness* of the grading.
She could not get over the *unfairness* of it.
The article documents the *unfairness* of the old system.

gloss: A feeling of sadness or dissatisfaction.
examples: There was obvious *unhappiness* among the staff.
He hid his *unhappiness* well.
The survey measured *unhappiness* with the new schedule.

gloss: An imaginary white horse with a single horn on its forehead.
examples: Her backpack is covered in *unicorns*.
The tapestry shows a *unicorn* in a walled garden.
In tech, a startup worth a billion dollars is called a *unicorn*.

gloss: The process of workers forming or joining a labor union.
examples: *Unionization* at the warehouse took two years.
The company fought *unionization* every step of the way.
*Unionization* rates have fallen since the 1970s.
contrast: American English spells it unionization; British English writes unionisation.

gloss: The state of doing or saying something at exactly the same time as others.
examples: The whole class answered in *unison*.
The dancers moved in perfect *unison*.
The choir sang the first verse in *unison*.

gloss: A big, sudden, and usually unsettling change.
examples: The merger caused months of *upheaval* at the office.
The country went through political *upheaval* after the election.
Her childhood was a series of *upheavals*.

gloss: A small increase in something.
examples: Hospitals reported an *uptick* in flu cases.
There was a modest *uptick* in sales last quarter.
Small *upticks* in traffic don't mean much.

gloss: An improvement, especially in business or the economy.
examples: Dealers are hoping for an *upturn* in the spring.
The *upturn* came later than economists predicted.
Past *upturns* have always followed a rate cut.

gloss: The process by which more and more people come to live in cities.
examples: Rapid *urbanization* has strained the water supply.
*Urbanization* changed the country in a single generation.
The map shows *urbanization* spreading along the coast.
contrast: American English spells it urbanization; British English writes urbanisation.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The act of using something, or a purpose that something can serve.
examples: The *use* of cell phones is banned during the exam.
This tool has a hundred *uses* around the house.
What's the *use* of arguing about it now?
contrast: The noun ends in an s sound, YOOS; the verb use ends in a z sound, YOOZ.
